issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: The trigger profile mixes tactile/startle-type cues and driving-with-others cues that could fit war-zone trauma, but 'being looked at sexually' points toward a sexual-threat trauma context that is not supported elsewhere in memory, threat, or appraisal items. This specific trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The dominant threat items describe generalized vigilance and fear of interpersonal attack. In combination with the sexual-objectification trigger, this pulls the profile toward an interpersonal/sexual trauma formulation, whereas the memory and appraisal items do not contain corresponding themes. This creates cross-node incoherence.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is not impossible, but in this profile it lacks a clear link to the other selected items. The rest of the appraisals center on unfairness, shame, and inability to trust oneself; without any role-related trauma content in memory, triggers, or threat, this item feels weakly anchored and clinically mismatched relative to the otherwise war-zone/interpersonal-danger presentation.

vignette:
Aroha Tane is a 46-year-old Māori woman, married and working as a veterinarian at a mixed-practice clinic in a mid-sized Pacific Northwest city. She presented for assessment following a referral from her primary care physician, who had grown concerned after Aroha disclosed during a routine appointment that she had not slept more than three consecutive hours in several months. Her PCL-5 score of 78 placed her firmly in the severe range, and the picture that emerged across the intake and early sessions was one of a woman whose internal world had been profoundly reorganised by events she witnessed and survived approximately eighteen months ago.

Aroha had travelled to a conflict-affected region of the Pacific as part of a humanitarian veterinary mission, supporting livestock health in communities displaced by ongoing fighting. On her third week in the field, the convoy she was travelling in was caught in crossfire between armed factions on a narrow road outside a rural settlement. The vehicle ahead of hers was struck. In the chaos that followed, the driver of Aroha's truck was killed beside her, slumping suddenly against her shoulder. She was pulled from the vehicle by a soldier whose language she did not speak, his hands gripping her arms without warning, dragging her across gravel into a drainage ditch where she lay for what she later estimated was close to two hours while the exchange of fire continued overhead. She could not move, could not help the wounded around her, and could not know whether the next moment would be her last.

In the weeks after she returned home to Oregon, Aroha noticed that her memories of those hours did not behave the way she expected memories to behave. They did not sit still. They arrived in pieces - the weight of the driver's body against her, the gravel under her palms, a particular quality of light - fragments that did not connect into a coherent sequence no matter how hard she tried to arrange them. When she attempted to recall the event more fully, what surfaced alongside those pieces was not grief or fear but something she struggled to name, something closer to shame. She had come to believe, in a way she found difficult to articulate but impossible to dismiss, that she had failed the people around her. That she had lain still and survived while others had not, and that this said something definitive about who she was.

She was certain, in a way that resisted all counter-evidence, that she could not be trusted to protect herself or anyone else. Bad things had happened to her once without warning and without her being able to stop them, and she had concluded that this would happen again. Nothing about her environment felt stable enough to contradict this. She scanned the waiting room of her clinic each morning when she arrived, noting exits, watching the body language of clients, alert to any shift in atmosphere she could not immediately explain. She could not relax in the examination rooms, even during routine appointments, even when nothing was wrong.

At work, the consequences had become concrete. During a farm call six months ago, a colleague placed a hand briefly on her shoulder to steady her on uneven ground, and Aroha's reaction - a sharp recoil, a gasp she could not suppress - had frightened them both. She had driven to farm visits alone ever since, arranging her schedule to avoid shared vehicles. The professional distance this created had not gone unnoticed, and she was aware that her colleagues had stopped asking her to accompany them. She had not explained why.

Loud sounds - a metal gate swinging shut, a dog kennel door slamming - produced a full-body response she could neither predict nor control, and she had begun arriving at the clinic before other staff to reduce the likelihood of encountering them unprepared.

At home, she lay beside her husband each night without sleeping, listening. She had told him very little. What finally brought her to seek help was not her own distress but his: he had asked her quietly one evening whether she still trusted him, and she had not been able to answer. What she feared most, sitting in the intake session, was that the answer was no - not because of anything he had done, but because she no longer trusted anything at all, including herself.
